why: Black's Qb4+ and Qxe4 threat was ignored, and c4 opened the b1-e4 line against a pinned, undefended e4 pawn.
Bd3 took the bishop off f1, which was the only guard of g2, so the queen takes it.
White's f4xe5 and Bxe6 threat was ignored; Bxb3 first removes the attacker.
d5 challenged the centre before the king was safe or pieces developed, letting exd5 open lines.
Qxg2# was threatened and h4 weakened the shelter instead of g3 covering g2.
The centre king faced Qb4+ with a mating net; cxd5 ignored it where Qd4+ forced a draw.
Nf7# was threatened and a5 did nothing about it; Qh5 captures the attacking knight's support.
Grabbing c7 cost time and ignored the c4 break that attacks d5 and the black kingside play.
In this rook ending the king went to g4 where it is checked, instead of staying behind the pawns to stop the passed pawns.
Nxc7 simply won an undefended pawn while the knight on b5 was also under threat, but Qb3+ lost the tempo.
Black's Nxc3 would remove the defender of e5; Bxe4 first prevents it, and castling left a back-rank weakness.
Black's Nxc4 trade left e5 weak; Bb3 first keeps the bishop and wins e5.
Bxa8 was threatened and Bb7 allowed a trade; Rd8 develops and brings the king toward safety.
Nh6+ put the knight on the rim, while Ne5+ keeps it central and blocks the b-pawn.
Qc7 puts the queen where a rook hits it with tempo; Bd4 keeps pieces coordinated.
